events.body:

claims.assertion: This was a metered RydeTAXI trip (Clarke Quay → Bedok Mall, $42.52 charged), so extra distance driven by the driver flows directly into the metered fare; the GPS track shows 20.1 km actual against a 15.5 km optimal route, i.e. +4.6 km (+30%).

There is one off-route segment, 12:46–13:07, in which 9.70 km was driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route; this is an unexempted detour under RD-1.

No chat agreement exists: there are no in-app messages at all, so the rider never agreed to any route change before the driver left the optimal route, and the driver's own statement admits he went off at Paya Lebar on his GPS without consulting the rider.

No traffic justification applies: no LTA incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, the expressways used were flowing at 60–69 km/h (band 7) and weather was fair, while the only slow record (Paya Lebar Road, band 3) is on the detour the driver chose, not on the replaced optimal leg.

The billable excess on the unexempted segment is 4.08 km; at the trip's own per-km rate of $1.41 (distance fare $28.31 ÷ 20.1 km), the rider should get $5.75 back (4.08 × $1.41, rounded to the cent), consistent with the fare sheet's valuation of the 4.6 km excess at $6.50.
The driver has 3 upheld route-deviation disputes in the last 90 days, so this upheld case makes his conduct 'repeated' and warrants referring his account to Ryde for review alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The GPS excess (F1, F3: +4.08 km) exceeds the fare sheet's billed excess distance valuation of 4.6 km × $1.41 = $6.50 (F4), so the driver may argue the metered fare already reflects the route the rider accepted and that any per-km refund should be capped or is redundant with the base/distance split in F6.

The payout is notional to the rider: under NS-7 any refund for this ride is issued as a Ryde voucher, not cash, and RD-2's per-km formula is itself an unpublished Ryde gap (G5), so the driver can contest the precise $5.75 figure.

Nothing in the record shows the rider objected during the 12:46–13:07 detour (F7: no chat at all), which the driver may use to argue acquiescence, though the absence of any driver notice (F8) is what actually defeats a RD-5 consent defence.

ruling.reasoning:
This is a metered RydeTAXI trip (Clarke Quay → Bedok Mall), so extra kilometres flow directly into the fare charged: $42.52 = base $3.90 + distance $28.31 for 20.1 km + time $8.84 + platform $1.47, with no surge [F5][F6]. Under RD-2's RydeTAXI branch the refund is limited to the metered distance of unexempted deviation segments, not the whole fare [F6][RD-2].

The GPS records show the trip ran 20.1 km against an optimal 15.5 km (+4.6 km, +30%), and one off-route segment is recorded, 12:46–13:07, driving 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km — an extra 4.08 km, straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route [F1][F3]. That segment is an unexempted deviation under RD-1 [F3][RD-1].

No exemption applies to that segment. RD-5 requires a driver route-change proposal made before leaving the optimal route plus the rider's clear agreement, and there is no in-app chat at all, hence no pre-departure agreement; the driver's own statement that he "followed my GPS, it took me off at Paya Lebar" confirms the reroute was never put to the rider [F7][F8][RD-5]. RD-3 fails for the same reason — no rider-named stop or rider-requested reroute exists [F7][RD-3]. RD-4 fails because no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only slow speed band (Paya Lebar Road, band 3, 12:45–13:15) sits on the road the driver actually drove, not on the replaced optimal leg, which ran at band 7 (60–69 km/h) on the PIE to 12:46; a speed band alone is corroborative and cannot exempt a segment [F9][F10][F11][F12][RD-4].

Applying the RD-2 formula to the sole unexempted segment: 4.08 extra_km × $1.4099/km (distance fare $28.31 ÷ 20.1 km) = $5.75 [F3][F6][RD-2]. The residual difference between the 4.6 km GPS gap and the 4.08 km segment (about 0.5 km) is map-matching residual and is not refunded under RD-2 [F1][F3][F4][RD-2]. Both advocates converge on this same figure, and the refund is issued as a Ryde voucher rather than cash [RD-2].

Because a refund greater than zero and an RD-1 violation are established by this case, and the driver's profile shows 3 upheld route-deviation disputes in the last 90 days — making this conduct "repeated" — RD-6 attaches the account-review referral; the profile facts are used only for that add-on, never to decide the deviation itself [F15][RD-6].

rejected_claims.reason: The claim that the route was permissible as the 'fastest or most efficient' is not borne out: no traffic incident was recorded near the route [F12], the replaced optimal leg ran free-flowing at band 7 (60–69 km/h) on the PIE to 12:46 [F10], and the only slow band (Paya Lebar Road band 3) lies on the detour itself [F11]; a lone speed band is corroborative only and cannot exempt a segment under RD-4(b), and RD-4(c) routes the segment to the RD-2 refund instead of exemption. A GPS-preferred route does not override the shortest-and-most-direct obligation where no reasonable cause is shown [RD-4][RD-1].

Accepted only in part and it does not reduce the refund: the 0.5 km residual between the 4.6 km GPS gap and the 4.08 km segment is indeed not refundable map-matching residual under RD-2 [F1][F3], but the rider claims exactly the 4.08 extra_km of the recorded segment, so the residual argument leaves the $5.75 figure unchanged [F3][RD-2].

Correct on the metered-fare structure and it is not resisted: the recoverable amount is limited to the unexempted segment's metered distance under RD-2's RydeTAXI branch, not the whole fare [F6][F5][RD-2]. This does not defeat the rider's claim, which sought only that distance element.

The driver's own concession that no RD-3/RD-5 exemption exists [F7][F8] confirms rather than rebuts the rider's case; the segment therefore stands as an unexempted deviation triggering RD-2 [RD-3][RD-5][RD-2].

The full +4.6 km GPS gap is not the refund measure: it includes about 0.5 km of map-matching residual above the 4.08 km recorded segment, which RD-2 excludes from the refundable amount [F1][F3][RD-2]. Only the segment's extra_km is refunded.

The RD-6 referral is an account-review add-on, not a basis for enlarging the refund; the profile facts support only the flag_account action and cannot increase the payable amount beyond the RD-2 computation [F15][RD-6].

events.title: Notices sent to rider and driver
events.body:
RIDER: We reviewed your Clarke Quay to Bedok Mall trip and found that part of the fare came from a detour that wasn't justified. The route you were driven was longer than the most direct option, and the extra distance on that stretch was added to your metered fare. We're refunding $5.75 for that extra distance, issued as a Ryde voucher on your account. Nothing else changes on your side, and you don't need to do anything — the voucher will appear in your Ryde wallet.

DRIVER: We reviewed the Clarke Quay to Bedok Mall trip and found that one stretch of the route was a deviation from the most direct path, and that this extra distance was charged to the rider. As a result, $5.75 of the fare is being refunded to the rider as a Ryde voucher. Because this trip adds to a pattern on your account, we're also referring your account to Ryde account review. A reviewer will look at your recent route history and how routes are chosen and explained to riders. You'll hear from us through the app.

actions.detail: account action is never automatic; queued for Ryde review

what_would_change: Had an LTA incident been recorded on the stretch F3 replaced, before it started, RD-4 would exempt it (−$5.75).

claims.assertion: This was a metered RydeTAXI trip (Clarke Quay → Bedok Mall, $42.52 charged), so extra distance driven by the driver flows directly into the metered fare; the GPS track shows 20.1 km actual against a 15.5 km optimal route, i.e. +4.6 km (+30%).

There is one off-route segment, 12:46–13:07, in which 9.70 km was driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route; this is an unexempted detour under RD-1.

No chat agreement exists: there are no in-app messages at all, so the rider never agreed to any route change before the driver left the optimal route, and the driver's own statement admits he went off at Paya Lebar on his GPS without consulting the rider.

No traffic justification applies: no LTA incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, the expressways used were flowing at 60–69 km/h (band 7) and weather was fair, while the only slow record (Paya Lebar Road, band 3) is on the detour the driver chose, not on the replaced optimal leg.

The billable excess on the unexempted segment is 4.08 km; at the trip's own per-km rate of $1.41 (distance fare $28.31 ÷ 20.1 km), the rider should get $5.75 back (4.08 × $1.41, rounded to the cent), consistent with the fare sheet's valuation of the 4.6 km excess at $6.50.
The driver has 3 upheld route-deviation disputes in the last 90 days, so this upheld case makes his conduct 'repeated' and warrants referring his account to Ryde for review alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The GPS excess (F1, F3: +4.08 km) exceeds the fare sheet's billed excess distance valuation of 4.6 km × $1.41 = $6.50 (F4), so the driver may argue the metered fare already reflects the route the rider accepted and that any per-km refund should be capped or is redundant with the base/distance split in F6.

The payout is notional to the rider: under NS-7 any refund for this ride is issued as a Ryde voucher, not cash, and RD-2's per-km formula is itself an unpublished Ryde gap (G5), so the driver can contest the precise $5.75 figure.

Nothing in the record shows the rider objected during the 12:46–13:07 detour (F7: no chat at all), which the driver may use to argue acquiescence, though the absence of any driver notice (F8) is what actually defeats a RD-5 consent defence.

claims.assertion: This is a RydeTAXI metered trip: the fare is per the taxi company's meter (base $3.90 + distance $28.31 for 20.1 km + time $8.84 for 34.0 min + platform $1.47 = $42.52, no surge 1.0x), so any refund is limited to the metered distance units of unexempted deviation km under the RD-2 RydeTAXI branch, not to the whole fare.

Only one off-route segment is recorded (12:46-13:07, 9.70 km driven vs 5.62 km optimal, +4.08 km), while the total GPS excess is 4.6 km; the residual difference (about 0.5 km) is not attributable to the recorded segment and, per RD-2, is map-matching residual that is not refunded.

The driver's route choice was made in live traffic conditions with no incident to justify or condemn it: PIE was flowing at band 7 (60-69 km/h) up to 12:46 but Paya Lebar Road was band 3 (20-29 km/h) 12:45-13:15, and no traffic incident was recorded near the route; the driver is permitted to pick the fastest or most efficient route per GPS, and RD-4(c) applies since no incident corroborates either a blockage defence or a free-flow alternative.

There was no in-app chat at all, so no passenger-designated stop, no pre-departure agreement and no passenger-named destination change can be shown to exempt the segment under RD-3(a) or RD-5; the deviation stands as unexempted.

Applying the RD-2 RydeTAXI formula to the only measured unexempted segment: refund = 4.08 extra_km x $1.41/km (fare distance fare $28.31 / 20.1 km) = $5.75, with the remaining $0.75 of the $6.50 billed excess distance not refundable as matching residual.

Because a refund greater than zero and an RD-1 violation are established in this case, and the driver's 90-day profile shows 3 upheld route disputes (5 disputes total in 90 days across 640 trips), RD-6 permits the additional account-review action alongside the partial refund; the profile facts are used only for that add-on and not to decide the deviation itself.

weaknesses: The core adverse facts are system records, not statements: F1 shows the trip ran 20.1 km against an optimal 15.5 km (+4.6 km, +30%) and F3 shows a single 21-minute off-route segment adding 4.08 km reaching 1720 m from the optimal route, so the deviation is objectively established and cannot be argued away by the driver's statement in F8.

No RD-3 or RD-5 exemption is available to the driver: F7 shows no in-app chat, so there was no passenger-named stop and no pre-departure agreement, and the rider's complaint expressly states the driver never asked.

No RD-4 defence survives: F12 records no traffic incident near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band evidence (F11, Paya Lebar Road band 3) sits on the road the driver actually used, not on the replaced optimal segment, so RD-4(b) cannot justify the reroute (and in any case is only corroborative, not a standalone exemption).
F15 (5 disputes, 3 upheld, 3 of them route-related in the last 90 days) invites the RD-6 flag_account referral against the driver.

points.response: Accepted: this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, so I do not seek the whole fare — only the metered distance attributable to the unexempted segment. The meter itself is the proof of loss: distance $28.31 was charged for 20.1 km against a 15.5 km optimal route (F6, F1), so every unexempted extra km is a per-km overcharge under RD-2's RydeTAXI branch.
Consistent with my claim C5 — I claim exactly the 4.08 extra_km of the recorded segment (F3), not the residual 0.5 km, which the fare sheet itself values separately (F4). No dispute on the residual.

This argument defeats itself: RD-4 requires traffic evidence about the replaced optimal leg, and F12 records no incident near the route while the optimal leg ran at 60-69 km/h band 7 on PIE up to 12:46 (F10) with fair weather (F13); the only slow record, Paya Lebar Road band 3 (F11), sits on the very detour the driver chose, so RD-4(c) routes the segment to my RD-2 refund rather than exempting it, and the driver's F8 statement cannot convert a free-flowing optimal route into a 'fastest or most efficient' one.

Agreed that the segment is unexempted — that is my case: F7 shows no chat, so there was no passenger-named stop or pre-departure agreement, and F3 shows the driver left the optimal route without any notice, leaving RD-1 breached and RD-2 triggered.

This matches my computed figure exactly, and RD-2 requires the refund to be measured from the unexempted segment's extra_km (F3) at the trip's per-km rate derived from F6, so $5.75 is the correct, fact-computable amount.

No objection: with a refund greater than zero and an RD-1 violation recorded, F15 (3 upheld route disputes in 90 days) supports the RD-6 flag_account referral, and the profile facts are used only for that add-on, never to decide the deviation itself.

Accepted, but it cuts against the rider's own framing: F6 shows the $42.52 is a metered breakdown (base $3.90 + distance $28.31 + time $8.84 + platform $1.47) with no surge (F5), so the recoverable amount is not the whole fare nor the 'almost 20 km' the rider complains of, but only the metered distance units of the unexempted segment under the RD-2 RydeTAXI branch.

Agreed that one unexempted segment exists under RD-1, but its measured contribution is 4.08 km (F3), not the 4.6 km GPS gap relied on in C1; under RD-2 the difference of roughly 0.5 km is residual that is not refunded.

Correct on consent — F7 shows no in-app messages, so no RD-5 pre-departure agreement and no RD-3(a) passenger-named stop exists, and the driver's F8 statement does not create one; I do not defend the segment as agreed.

No RD-4 exemption is claimed: F12 records no incident near the route, and the only slow band (F11, Paya Lebar Road, band 3) is on the leg the driver actually drove, not the replaced optimal leg, so RD-4(b) cannot exempt the segment either.

The arithmetic uses my own RD-2 formula and the same $1.41/km from F4/F6, so $5.75 on 4.08 extra km stands, and it is deliberately below the $6.50 the fare sheet ascribes to the full 4.6 km excess (F1, F4) — the $0.75 gap is matching residual that RD-2 leaves with the driver.

I do not resist the referral: with 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days (F15) an RD-6 flag_account addition is available, and I note it is an account-review add-on, not a larger refund — the payment remains the $5.75 computed in D5 from F3/F4/F6.
